paras: The shooting of Manning Law took place in late October 1881 near Buck Creek, South Carolina, when the two brothers of Mary Lewis, a white woman of Lexington County, overtook her and her new husband, a Black man, as the couple drove toward Augusta, Georgia. Law was shot in the breast in an exchange of pistol fire, and the brothers then hunted the preacher who had married the couple. Papers across the country carried the story as a case of "miscegenation," with conflicting reports on whether Law died.

According to a special dispatch from Columbia dated October 28, Mary Lewis married "a coal-black negro named Manning Law" that morning, and the couple set out for Augusta in a buggy. The dispatch described her as "very well connected," and a Virginia brief added that she belonged to "a respectable family" and was "accomplished." The Chicago Tribune said the ceremony was "performed as privately as possible."

Her two brothers went after the pair and caught up with them at "a point called Buck Creek," which the Tribune placed about ten miles along the road. In the preacher's account, Law, "apprehending death at the hands of his pursuers," drew a pistol and fired first; the brothers returned the fire and one shot struck him in the breast. The dispatch called the wound one that "will probably prove mortal."

The brothers then went to the house of the preacher who had performed the ceremony and threatened to kill him. He ran into the woods with the brothers firing after him, hid in a thicket, and took the night train to Columbia, where he told a correspondent what had happened.

The Columbia dispatch closed by saying it was not known whether Law had died or what had become of his wife and her brothers. No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution of the brothers appears in the coverage, and no later word on Law was found.

The story reached the press through the preacher, first as a Chicago Tribune special on October 29 and in a condensed Columbia dispatch dated the same day. Within two weeks it had run in papers in Virginia, Tennessee, West Virginia, Illinois, Minnesota and Wisconsin, and in South Carolina's Keowee Courier, which reprinted the Tribune's version. As it was shortened, Law's condition hardened from "probably mortal" to "fatally wounded" and then to "Law was killed."

Headline writers framed the case around the marriage rather than the shooting: the Memphis Public Ledger titled it "Miscegenation, And Murder as a Purifier of a Stained Family Record," and the Ottawa Free Trader "Perils of Miscegenation." The Ottawa paper remarked that couples who defied popular opinion were "pretty certain to be brought before Judge Lynch and punished without ceremony or mercy." A Chicago Tribune editorial paragraph treated the affair with sarcasm, mocking the "sanguinary brothers" and the South Carolina "gentleman of the old school" who erased a family stain with a revolver, while calling Law a "dusky person" who had forced himself into the family. Midwestern news summaries reduced it to a single line reporting that the brothers "killed the dusky bridegroom."

The reports disagree on Law's fate: the original dispatch and its Memphis reprint left it unknown, the Richmond Dispatch and the Tribune editorial called him fatally wounded or dying, and the West Virginia Argus and Mower County Transcript said he was killed. The "killed" versions are condensations of the same story with no new source, so the fuller original is the better evidence. The date of the marriage also varies, between the morning of the October 28 dispatch (a Friday) and the Richmond Dispatch's "Thursday last."

reader.title: Shooting of Manning Law
bases: Two brothers of a white woman pursued her and her Black husband after their marriage and shot him in an exchange of fire, then shot at the officiating preacher (A2, A8); two named kin acting together fit neither a mob nor an organized band.

The attackers were 'the two irate brothers' of the bride, not a group of three or more (A2), and whether Law died is unsettled: the original dispatch called the wound probably mortal and his fate unknown (A2), while condensed versions said he was killed (A5, A8); the papers framed the shooting as erasing a family 'stain' over an interracial marriage (A3, A7).

Every version, including the separate Columbia dispatch of Oct. 29 (A8) and the Richmond brief (A4), traces to the preacher's account given in Columbia (A2, A10); no local report, statement from the brothers, or word of Law's death or survival was found.

accounts.label: Preacher's account (Columbia special dispatch, Oct. 28)
accounts.gist: Law, fearing death, fired first when overtaken; the fire was returned and he was shot in the breast with a wound that would 'probably prove mortal'; it was not known whether he died.

accounts.label: Condensed Columbia dispatch (Oct. 29)
accounts.gist: Law, 'apprehending violence', fired; the fire was returned 'and Law was killed'; the preacher escaped to Columbia.

accounts.label: Richmond / Stephens City brief
accounts.gist: Married 'Thursday last'; Law opened fire on sight of the brothers and was 'fatally wounded'; the preacher was chased into the woods under fire.

accounts.label: News-summary item (Mower County, Watertown)
accounts.gist: The brothers pursued the couple 'and killed the dusky bridegroom'.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune editorial mocked the 'sanguinary brothers' and the 'gentleman of the old school' who erases a family 'stain' with 'the persuasive revolver', while calling Law a 'dusky person who had with such bad taste forced himself into their family'.
The Memphis Public Ledger ran the dispatch under 'Miscegenation, And Murder as a Purifier of a Stained Family Record.'
The Ottawa Free Trader's 'Perils of Miscegenation' observed that couples defying popular opinion were 'pretty certain to be brought before Judge Lynch' without 'ceremony or mercy'.
Brief news summaries in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Virginia and West Virginia ran the item flatly among other crimes, under heads such as 'Tragical Tales' and 'A Southern Episode'.

versions.value: Wound 'will probably prove mortal'; not known whether he died

conflicts.note: The fullest and earliest account, from the preacher, says his fate was unknown; the 'killed' versions are later condensations of the same story with no new source, so the death is not established.
The original dispatch is internally loose, saying the marriage took place 'This morning' while the preacher reached Columbia 'Last night late' (A2).
Not necessarily inconsistent; the editorial rewrite drops the place name.

info: The marriage and pursuit took place on the morning the Columbia dispatch was written, Oct. 28, 1881 ('This morning'; 'Friday morning'); the Richmond brief instead dates the marriage 'Thursday last' (Oct. 27).
The couple were overtaken at 'a point called Buck Creek' on the road toward Augusta, Ga.; the Tribune editorial puts it 'about ten miles' on their journey.
Manning Law, described as 'a coal-black negro' or 'a colored man', was shot; the preacher who married the couple was pursued and fired at but escaped.
No crime was alleged; the provocation reported was the marriage of a white woman to a Black man.
The two brothers of Mary Lewis (called 'the Lewis brothers'); not named individually.
Unclear: two condensed versions say Law was killed; the original dispatch says it was not known whether he died.
At last report the preacher had reached Columbia by night train; Law's fate and what became of Mary Lewis and her brothers were unknown.
